Municipal Water Treatment: An Overview of Regulatory Requirements

Public water systems in the United States operate under the Safe Drinking Water Act, which Congress passed in 1974 and amended in 1986 and 1996. The Act authorizes the Environmental Protection Agency to set national standards for contaminants that may be present in drinking water. A public water system is defined as any system that provides water for human consumption to at least 15 service connections or regularly serves at least 25 people for 60 or more days each year. Most states have accepted primary enforcement authority, which is called primacy, and they administer the federal rules through their own drinking water programs.

Each regulated contaminant receives a maximum contaminant level goal and, in most cases, an enforceable maximum contaminant level. The goal is the level below which there is no known or expected risk to health, and it is not enforceable. The maximum contaminant level is the highest level of a contaminant that is allowed in drinking water, and it is set as close to the goal as feasible after considering cost and available treatment technology. When it is not economically or technically feasible to measure a contaminant, the agency may instead require a treatment technique, which is a required process intended to reduce the level of that contaminant.

Source water quality varies widely between systems. Surface water drawn from rivers, lakes and reservoirs is exposed to runoff and generally carries more particles and microorganisms than groundwater. Groundwater pumped from aquifers is usually clearer, but it can contain dissolved iron, manganese, arsenic or nitrate. Groundwater that is under the direct influence of surface water is regulated in the same way as surface water because it can carry the same pathogens. Utilities are expected to understand their watershed and to identify potential sources of contamination through a source water assessment.

Conventional treatment of surface water follows a sequence of steps. Coagulation is the addition of chemicals such as aluminum sulfate or ferric chloride, which neutralize the electrical charge on suspended particles. Flocculation follows coagulation, and gentle mixing causes the destabilized particles to collide and form larger clumps called floc. During sedimentation, the water moves slowly through a basin so that the heavy floc settles to the bottom as sludge. Filtration then removes the remaining particles as water passes through layers of sand, anthracite coal or granular activated carbon. Disinfection is the final barrier, and it inactivates the pathogens that survived the earlier steps.

Turbidity is a measure of the cloudiness of water caused by suspended particles, and it is reported in nephelometric turbidity units. High turbidity matters because particles can shield microorganisms from disinfectants. Under the Interim Enhanced Surface Water Treatment Rule, systems using conventional or direct filtration must keep combined filter effluent turbidity at or below 0.3 NTU in at least 95 percent of the measurements taken each month. Combined filter effluent may never exceed 1 NTU. Operators typically record turbidity every four hours, and many plants now use continuous online turbidimeters on each individual filter.

Microbial treatment requirements are expressed as log removal or inactivation. A 3 log reduction means that 99.9 percent of the target organisms have been removed or inactivated. Surface water systems must achieve at least 3 log removal or inactivation of Giardia lamblia cysts and 4 log removal or inactivation of viruses. Filtration earns a portion of this credit, and disinfection must provide the rest. The Long Term 2 Enhanced Surface Water Treatment Rule added requirements for Cryptosporidium, a protozoan parasite that is highly resistant to chlorine. Systems with higher Cryptosporidium concentrations in their source water are placed in higher treatment bins and must add more treatment, such as ultraviolet light or membrane filtration.

Chlorine remains the most common disinfectant in municipal systems because it is inexpensive and leaves a lasting residual in the distribution system. The effectiveness of chlorine is described by the CT concept, which is the product of the disinfectant concentration in milligrams per liter and the contact time in minutes. A higher pH reduces the effectiveness of free chlorine, so operators must account for pH when they calculate the required contact time. Chloramine, formed by combining chlorine with ammonia, is a weaker disinfectant but persists longer in large distribution networks. Ozone and ultraviolet light are strong primary disinfectants, but neither leaves a residual, so systems that use them still add chlorine or chloramine before water enters the distribution system.

Disinfection creates its own risks. When chlorine reacts with natural organic matter in the water, it forms disinfection byproducts, including trihalomethanes and haloacetic acids. Long term exposure to these byproducts has been associated with an increased risk of cancer. The Stage 2 Disinfectants and Disinfection Byproducts Rule sets a maximum contaminant level of 0.080 milligrams per liter for total trihalomethanes and 0.060 milligrams per liter for the five regulated haloacetic acids. Compliance is based on a locational running annual average, which means that the average at each individual monitoring location must meet the standard. Utilities often reduce byproduct formation by removing organic matter before disinfection, a practice known as enhanced coagulation.

The rules also limit how much disinfectant may remain in the water. The maximum residual disinfectant level for chlorine is 4.0 milligrams per liter, measured as a running annual average of samples from the distribution system. At the same time, systems must maintain a detectable residual throughout the distribution system, because a residual protects against contamination that enters through main breaks or cross connections. Balancing these two requirements is a routine challenge for operators, particularly at the far ends of large systems where water age is high.

Lead in drinking water usually comes from service lines, solder and plumbing fixtures rather than from the source. The Lead and Copper Rule therefore relies on corrosion control rather than a conventional maximum contaminant level. Under the original rule, the action level for lead was 15 parts per billion, measured at the 90th percentile of tap samples taken from high risk homes. Copper has an action level of 1.3 milligrams per liter. When a system exceeds an action level, it must take further steps, which may include optimizing corrosion control treatment, educating the public and replacing lead service lines. Corrosion control often involves adjusting pH and alkalinity or adding orthophosphate, which forms a protective scale on the inside of pipes.

Monitoring requirements depend on the size of the system and the type of source. The Total Coliform Rule, later revised, requires systems to collect routine samples from the distribution system each month. Coliform bacteria are used as indicator organisms because their presence suggests that the system may be vulnerable to contamination. If a sample tests positive for Escherichia coli, the system must act quickly, because E. coli indicates recent fecal contamination. A positive result can trigger repeat sampling, an assessment of the system and, in serious cases, a boil water advisory.

Public notification is required whenever a system violates a standard or a monitoring requirement. Notices are divided into three tiers based on the risk to health. A Tier 1 notice is required for situations with significant potential for serious health effects from short term exposure, and it must be delivered within 24 hours. Tier 2 notices cover other violations with potential health effects and must be given within 30 days. Tier 3 notices cover monitoring and reporting violations and may be included in the annual report. That annual report is called the Consumer Confidence Report, and community water systems must deliver it to their customers by July 1 of each year.

Operators play a central role in compliance. Most states require that treatment plants and distribution systems be run by certified operators, and certification levels are tied to the complexity of the facility. Operators must complete continuing education to renew their certification. Recordkeeping is part of the job, and systems must keep bacteriological records for at least five years and chemical analysis records for at least ten years. Inspectors review these records during a sanitary survey, which is an onsite review of the source, facilities, equipment, operation and maintenance of a public water system.

Funding for compliance comes from several places. Water rates paid by customers cover most operating costs, while capital projects are often financed through bonds or low interest loans. The Drinking Water State Revolving Fund, created by the 1996 amendments, provides federal capitalization grants to states, which then lend the money to eligible systems. Because repaid loans return to the fund, the program can support new projects year after year. Small systems face the greatest difficulty because their fixed costs are spread across few customers, which leads to higher costs per household.
